facts.statement: The only known species, Concornis lacustris, is known from a single fairly complete skeleton.
facts.quote: The single known species, Concornis lacustris, was described from the remains of one fairly complete individual skeleton.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen MCCM-LH-1184 was first described in 1992 while still partially covered in sandstone.
facts.quote: The holotype of Concornis, MCCM-LH-1184 (also known as LH-2814) was initially described in 1992, while the specimen was still partially covered in sandstone.

facts.statement: A large redescription of the specimen was published in 1995 after further preparation was completed.
facts.quote: A large redescription was published in 1995 once further preparation concluded.

facts.statement: Fossils of Concornis are found in the Calizas de La Huérgina Formation at Las Hoyas, Cuenca province, Spain.
facts.quote: Its remains are known from the Calizas de La Huérgina Formation at Las Hoyas, Cuenca province, Spain.

facts.statement: Concornis lived during the late Barremian age of the early Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago.
facts.quote: Concornis is a genus of enantiornithean birds which lived during the early Cretaceous period, in the late Barremian age about 125 million years ago.

facts.statement: Concornis had an estimated wingspan of 34 centimeters and a weight of about 70 grams.
facts.quote: Concornis was an averaged sized enantiornithean, with an estimated wingspan of 34 centimeters (13 inches) and an estimated weight of about 70 g (2.5 oz).

facts.statement: Although the skull is unknown, Concornis almost certainly had teeth in a snout rather than a beak.
facts.quote: Its skull is unknown, but it almost certainly retained teeth in a snout (as in most other enantiornitheans) rather than a beak.

facts.statement: The known specimen is almost complete, missing only the skull, neck, and pygostyle.
facts.quote: The specimen is almost complete, only missing a few elements such as the skull, neck, and pygostyle.

facts.statement: Concornis had fairly long legs with a large hallux, neither specialized for perching nor for running.
facts.quote: The legs were fairly long and neither dedicated to perching on branches nor to running on the ground; it had a large hallux as is generally absent in terrestrial birds.

facts.statement: A 2018 study analyzed Concornis proportions to determine its optimal flight pattern.
facts.quote: A 2018 study analyzed the proportions of Concornis and Eoalulavis (a contemporary enantiornithean) to determine the optimal flight pattern for those genera.

facts.statement: Research suggests Concornis likely engaged in bounding flight, a pattern seen in modern small birds.
facts.quote: The study found that they likely engaged in bounding flight, a form of flight popular among modern small and short-winged birds.

facts.statement: Studies indicate Concornis could perform continuous flapping flight but was likely unable to glide due to its high body mass to wingspan ratio.
facts.quote: The study also found that they were capable of continuous flapping flight, but were likely unable to glide due to having a high body mass to wingspan ratio.

facts.statement: A 2008 analysis placed Concornis in the family Avisauridae based on features of the tibiotarsus.
facts.quote: A 2008 analysis placed Concornis in the family Avisauridae due to several features of the tibiotarsus (shinbone and upper ankle bones).

facts.statement: Under the Avisauridae classification, Concornis is the oldest and most complete member of the family.
facts.quote: Under this classification, Concornis is the oldest (and the most complete) member of the family.

facts.statement: A relationship with Sinornis and Cathayornis has been suggested based on a unique Y-shaped sternum with deep notches.
facts.quote: A relationship with Sinornis and Cathayornis has been suggested mainly based on a peculiarly autapomorphic sternum.

facts.statement: Despite its early age, Concornis appears to be a fairly derived member of Enantiornithes.
facts.quote: In fact, despite its early age, C. lacustris seems to be a fairly derived member of Enantiornithes.

facts.statement: Concornis lived during the late Barremian age of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 127 to 125 million years ago.
facts.quote: Vivió durante el Cretácico inferior, en la edad Barremiense superior, hace aproximadamente 127-125 millones de años

facts.statement: Concornis was a small bird with an approximate length of 13 centimeters and no tail.
facts.quote: Era un ave más bien pequeña, tenía aproximadamente 13 cm de longitud, sin cola.

facts.statement: The estimated weight of Concornis is between 75 and 100 grams.
facts.quote: Su peso se estima comprendido entre 75 y 100 g.

facts.statement: Concornis had a large hallux, a trait generally absent in terrestrial birds.
facts.quote: Tenía un gran hallux , rasgo generalmente ausente en aves terrestres.

facts.statement: The time range for Concornis is the Barremian, from 125.77 to 121.4 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Barremian (125.77 to 121.4 million years ago)

facts.statement: It is unknown whether Concornis had an alula, though it is likely present based on other enantiornitheans.
facts.quote: It is not known whether it had an alula, although it is likely as such a feature is present in other enantiornitheans such as Eoalulavis.

facts.statement: Concornis is sometimes considered a member of Enantiornithiformes and related to Enantiornis.
facts.quote: Es en ocasiones considerado como un miembro de Enantiornithiformes y relacionado con Enantiornis.

facts.statement: A cladistic analysis placed Concornis in Cathayornithiformes, grouping it with Sinornis and surprisingly with Neuquenornis volans, which belongs to a different lineage of Euenantiornithes.
facts.quote: Un análisis cladístico que incluyó a muchos taxones de enantiornites lo situó en "Cathayornithiformes", agrupándolo con Sinornis (o Cathayornis) y, sorprendentemente, Neuquenornis volans el cual fue considerado como perteneciente a un linaje distinto de Euenantiornithes.
